\section[Practice]{Review — three letters}

\label{lesson:ES-C54-repaso-hay}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new. What does \emph{hay} agree with?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
one thing & \emph{Hay una casa.} & There is a house. \\
many things & \emph{Hay libros.} & There are books. \\
an obligation & \emph{Hay que comer.} & One must eat. \\
what it is made of & \emph{ha} + \emph{y} & \textquotedblleft{}it has there\textquotedblright{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three letters, and everything above came out of them.

Notice the shape of this arc, because it is the shape of a lot of language learning: \textbf{the smallest words need the most explaining.} \emph{Hay} is shorter than any noun you have learned and it took four chapters, while \emph{comida} took one. Short words are short because they are used constantly, and constant use is what wears them into fossils that no longer explain themselves.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what it does not do}]
Two things \emph{hay} never does, and both save you work:

1. \textbf{It never agrees.} Not with number, not with anything. One form. 2. \textbf{It never names anybody.} Neither does \emph{hay que}.

So of everything you have learned about making Spanish verbs match their surroundings — six endings a tense, gender on the pronouns, number on the articles — none of it applies here. After a hundred and seventy chapters of agreement, the last word is the one that opted out.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} all four rows of the table
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Three uses of \emph{hay} — say them. (\emph{There is}, \emph{there are}, and \emph{\textbf{hay que}} for must.) What does it agree with? (\textbf{Nothing at all.}) Next: the last synthesis.
\end{tcolorbox}
